lesson.title: Exact logarithms
lesson.body:
logb x asks: "b to what power gives x?" When x is a power of b, just count.

  • log2 64 = 6 because 26 = 64. log5 125 = 3.
  • Reciprocals give negatives: log2(1/8) = −3, log10 0.001 = −3.
  • Roots give fractions: √x = x1/2, so log2 √32 = 5/2.

Fractional answers — rewrite both numbers as powers of a common root. If b = rp and x = rq, then logb x = q/p.

Example: log8 4. 8 = 23, 4 = 22 → 2/3. Check: 82/3 = (∛8)2 = 22 = 4. ✓

Example: log9(1/3). 9 = 32, 1/3 = 3−1 → −1/2.

Your powers-of-2 table (to 220) and cubes do most of the work: spot the root first (2, 3, 5, 10), then read off the two exponents. Type answers as fractions (2/3) or decimals (0.667).

lesson.title: Common logarithms
lesson.body:
Step 1 — scientific notation. log(a × 10k) = k + log a, so only the mantissa a (between 1 and 10) needs thought: log 3 000 = 3 + 0.477 = 3.477; log 0.0007 = −4 + 0.845 = −3.155.

Step 2 — factor the mantissa into digits. Logs turn × into + and ÷ into −:

  • 4.8 = 6 × 8 / 10 → 0.778 + 0.903 − 1 = 0.681
  • 2.5 = 10 / 4 → 1 − 0.602 = 0.398; 1.75 = 7 / 4 → 0.845 − 0.602 = 0.243

Step 3 — anything else: nearest anchor + linear correction. log(a + Δ) ≈ log a + 0.434 · Δ/a (0.434 = log e, the slope of ln converted to log). Use the closest number you can log exactly; keep Δ/a under ~5 % and the error is tiny.

Example: log 6 130 = 3 + log 6.13. Nearest anchor 6 (0.778); Δ/a = 0.13/6 ≈ 0.022; × 0.434 ≈ 0.009 → 3.787 (true 3.7875).

Example: log 1.3 — the digit 1 is too far, but 1.25 = 10/8 has log 1 − 0.903 = 0.097; 0.434 × 0.05/1.25 ≈ 0.017 → 0.114 (true 0.1139).

Useful extra anchors: 1.2 (0.079), 1.25 (0.097), 1.4 (0.146), 1.5 (0.176), 1.6 (0.204), 1.8 (0.255).

lesson.title: Powers of ten
lesson.body:
Reverse a log: 10x = 10fraction × 10integer. Take the integer part down (floor), so the fractional part is always between 0 and 1: 10−2.523 = 100.477 × 10−3.

Read the mantissa off your log table. 0.477 = log 3, so 103.477 ≈ 3 000 and 10−2.523 ≈ 0.003. 0.5 → √10 ≈ 3.16.

In between: nearest anchor, then correct linearly. If the fraction is d above log a, 10fraction ≈ a·(1 + d/0.434) — i.e. add a × d/0.434 (each 0.01 of log is about 2.3 %).

Example: 104.63. 0.63 is 0.028 above log 4 = 0.602 → 4 + 4 × 0.028/0.434 ≈ 4 + 0.26 = 4.26 → 42 600 (true 42 658).

Example: 100.18: no digit is close, but log 1.5 = 0.477 − 0.301 = 0.176, so ≈ 1.5 × (1 + 0.004/0.434) ≈ 1.51.

Low fractions need the factored anchors: 0.079 → 1.2, 0.097 → 1.25, 0.146 → 1.4, 0.176 → 1.5, 0.204 → 1.6, 0.255 → 1.8. Answer in any form: 42600, 4.26e4, 4.26x10^4.

lesson.title: Natural logarithms
lesson.body:
Factor into 2, 3, 5, 7, 10 and e and add the memorized logs (ln 2 = 0.693, ln 3 = 1.099, ln 5 = 1.609, ln 7 = 1.946, ln 10 = 2.303, ln e = 1):

  • ln 12 = 2 ln 2 + ln 3 = 1.386 + 1.099 = 2.485
  • ln 700 = ln 7 + 2 ln 10 = 1.946 + 4.606 = 6.552
  • ln 0.25 = −2 ln 2 = −1.386; ln(3e2) = 1.099 + 2 = 3.099

Anything else: anchor + Δ/a. The slope of ln at a is 1/a, so ln(a + Δ) ≈ ln a + Δ/a. Pull out powers of ten first (each adds 2.303), then pick the nearest number you can factor.

Example: ln 3 700 = ln 3.7 + 3 × 2.303. ln 3.7 ≈ ln 3.5 + 0.2/3.5, with ln 3.5 = ln 7 − ln 2 = 1.253 → 1.253 + 0.057 = 1.310; + 6.909 = 8.219 (true 8.216).

Alternative: ln x = 2.303 × log x, handy if you already know log x (ln 50 = 2.303 × 1.699 ≈ 3.91).

lesson.title: Change of base
lesson.body:
logb x = log x / log b — any base, using common logs you can already do.

Example: log3 50 = 1.699 / 0.477 ≈ 3.56. Sanity check: 33 = 27, 34 = 81, and 50 sits between. ✓

Base 2 shortcut. 210 = 1 024 ≈ 103, so log2 10 ≈ 3.32 (exactly 1/0.301 = 3.322). Then

  • log2 106 = 6 × 3.322 = 19.93 (220 ≈ a million ✓)
  • log2 5 000 = log2 5 + 3 × 3.322 = 2.322 + 9.966 = 12.29
  • log2 0.01 = −2 × 3.322 = −6.64

Worth knowing: log2 3 = 1.585, log2 5 = 2.322, log2 7 = 2.807 (each = log d / 0.301).

For bases that aren't digits, log the base like any other number: log 13 = 1 + log 1.3 ≈ 1.114. Keep three decimals in both logs before dividing — the division magnifies errors when log b is small.
